content: To upload an image, the file must first be uploaded to the system. This process is governed by legal copyright rules and may also be subject to specific site regulations. Other types of files can also be uploaded, and the system uses the term image to refer to any uploaded file. When uploading, it is important to choose a suitable file name, as renaming after uploading is not possible. Ensure the file name includes the correct extension. During the upload process, you can specify a destination file name, which does not need to match the local file name. Additionally, an upload summary can be provided. Once uploaded, the file will have an associated image page, also known as an image description page, with a name consisting of the file name (including its extension) prefixed by Image: or the equivalent namespace variable. File names are case-sensitive, including the extension, except for the first character in most projects. In Wikimedia projects, files are often uploaded to Wikimedia Commons, a shared repository for free content (excluding fair use content). This allows files to be used across multiple projects. To upload a file to Commons, log in to Commons and use the upload link provided. If you wish to replace an existing file, use the same name. Otherwise, choose a unique name. When replacing or deleting an image on Commons, all projects using that image will be affected. Therefore, it is crucial to link the Commons image page to the local image pages of all projects using it. Even if these local pages have not been explicitly created, the image links section will display the local pages that use the image. Select an image name as carefully as you would for an article, using proper spacing and capitalization. Avoid using a name already in use on any project unless the new image is intended to replace the local ones, which will then be deleted. Uploading an image locally has disadvantages, such as the inability to use it in other projects and potential conflicts with existing or future images of the same name on Commons. Local uploads should only be done for specific reasons, such as replacing a Commons image with a local version without altering the links. For embedding internal images, the system assumes the image name refers to one in the same project if it exists there; otherwise, it refers to one on Commons. If neither exists, a link to the upload page appears. Embedded internal images automatically link to the image page, which provides information about the image and may display a reduced version with a link to the full version, depending on user preferences. To add an uploaded image to an article as a thumbnail, use the appropriate syntax. The default thumbnail width can be set in user preferences, so it is generally better not to specify px unless a specific size is required. Captions can include links, and both the image and an icon link to the image page. The icon's hoverbox displays Enlarge, even if the image on the image page is smaller. For images positioned to the left or right, text will float around the image. The behavior of subsequent images depends on the presence of intervening text. Inline images cannot have captions but can include a title attribute, which appears in the hoverbox. The size of images can be adjusted, and examples of different link styles are available for reference. The gallery tag allows for the display of thumbnails in four columns, with each entry including the image name and an optional caption. A title can also be added to the gallery. Note that images in a gallery have a fixed width, and long captions may affect the layout depending on the browser. Before uploading, ensure you have the rights to upload and redistribute the image(s) and that they comply with Wikimedia Commons licensing requirements. Use descriptive file names to avoid confusion. Note that others may edit or delete your uploads if deemed necessary for the project, and you may be blocked from uploading if you abuse the system. When uploading a file with the same name as an existing one, the old file will be replaced. To avoid unintentional overwriting, check in advance that the name does not already exist. Supported file types include images (preferred formats: PNG, JPEG, GIF), sound files (preferred format: Ogg Vorbis), and others. For security reasons, some file types that were previously allowed may no longer be uploaded, but existing files can still be used. The maximum upload size is typically limited by server settings. For troubleshooting, ensure the file is not corrupt and has the correct extension. If issues persist, check for server or browser limitations. Use the upload log and image list to monitor changes to uploaded files.
